title: UML State & Activity Diagrams
summary: Two UML diagram types for behavior-over-decisions, distinct from a sequence diagram's behavior-over-time — drawn when a design has real states or real branching, not by default.

slides.markdown:
A sequence diagram answers "who calls whom, in what order." **State diagrams** and **activity diagrams** answer two different questions: "what state is this entity in right now, and what can move it to another state" and "what happens next in this process, including the branches."

Both are drawn far less often than class diagrams — reach for them only when an entity has genuinely non-trivial states or a process has genuinely interesting branching, never as a default addition to a design.

slides.sectionTitle: State diagrams: states, transitions, and guard conditions as their own notation
slides.markdown:
A **state diagram** models one object across its lifetime as a set of rounded-rectangle **states** connected by arrows called **transitions**, each labeled with the event that triggers it — `pay()`, `ship()`, `cancel()`. A transition can carry a **guard condition** in square brackets, like `cancel() [not yet shipped]`, restricting when it's allowed to fire.

This is a different notation family from class diagrams — it has nothing to say about attributes or methods, only about the finite set of states one object can be in and the legal moves between them. If you find yourself drawing multiplicities or a diamond on a state diagram, you've mixed notations by mistake.

This pairs directly with the **state design pattern**, which is the code-level implementation of exactly this diagram: one class per state, each handling transitions differently.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: a state diagram for an order lifecycle, transitions labeled with triggering events
slides.markdown:
```
(start) --> [Created]

[Created]  --pay()-->            [Paid]
[Paid]     --ship()-->           [Shipped]
[Shipped]  --deliver()-->        [Delivered] --> (end)
[Created]  --cancel()-->         [Cancelled] --> (end)
[Paid]     --cancel() [not yet shipped]--> [Cancelled]
```

Each arrow is one legal transition, and each label is the event that causes it — not a description, an actual trigger. Notice the guard on the second `cancel()`: once `[Shipped]`, there's no `cancel()` transition out of it at all, meaning cancellation after shipping simply isn't a modeled state change — a real design decision made visible by what's *absent* from the diagram.

![UML state diagram of an order lifecycle with a start dot into Created, transitions labelled pay(), ship(), deliver(), cancel() with a guard, and Delivered and Cancelled as final states](assets/order-state-diagram.svg)

slides.sectionTitle: Activity diagrams: swimlanes, decision nodes, and fork/join for a branching process
slides.markdown:
An **activity diagram** models a process as a flow of actions rather than one object's states. **Swimlanes** are parallel columns, one per actor or system, showing who performs each step — useful when a process crosses ownership boundaries, like a request moving from a `Requester` to a `Manager` to `Finance`. A **decision node** (diamond) branches the flow based on a condition, with each outgoing arrow labeled with the branch it represents. A **fork** splits one flow into concurrent parallel flows; a matching **join** waits for all of them to finish before continuing.

Fork/join is the one piece of notation genuinely unique to activity diagrams — neither state nor sequence diagrams have a native way to say "these two things happen at the same time and we wait for both." Reach for it specifically when a process has real independent parallel work, not just multiple sequential steps.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: an activity diagram for a multi-step approval workflow with a decision branch
slides.markdown:
```
(start)
   |
   v
[Submit request]
   |
   v
<Manager approves?> --No--> [Notify: rejected] --> (end)
   | Yes
   v
<Cost over $10k?> --No--> [Provision access] --> (end)
   | Yes
   v
[Finance review] --> <Finance approves?> --No--> [Notify: rejected] --> (end)
                              | Yes
                              v
                       [Provision access] --> (end)
```

The two decision diamonds are doing the real work here: a small request skips finance entirely, while a large one needs a second approval. This is exactly the shape of diagram to draw when an interviewer asks "walk me through the approval flow" — the branches *are* the answer, not a detail attached to it.

![UML activity diagram for an access-request approval with two decision diamonds for manager approval and cost threshold, routing through finance review when needed](assets/access-request-activity.svg)

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: state diagram vs activity diagram vs sequence diagram
slides.markdown:
| | State diagram | Activity diagram | Sequence diagram |
|---|---|---|---|
| Question answered | What state am I in? | What happens next? | Who calls whom? |
| Subject | One object's lifecycle | A process, possibly across actors | Messages between multiple objects |
| Key notation | States + labeled transitions | Decision diamonds, fork/join, swimlanes | Lifelines + ordered messages |
| Draw it when | An entity has non-trivial states and transitions | A process has real branching or parallel work | Interaction order or timing is the crux |

**How to decide:** ask what the interviewer's question is actually about. "Is" (a status) points to state; "then what" (a process) points to activity; "who talks to whom" points to sequence. Most designs need at most one of the three, not all — picking the wrong one wastes the diagram entirely.

slides.sectionTitle: When a state diagram earns its place: a genuinely stateful entity with non-trivial transitions
slides.markdown:
A state diagram earns its place when an entity has states that (a) restrict which transitions are legal from each other state, and (b) have distinct behavior attached to being in that state — not just a label. An `Order` qualifies: you can't `ship()` before `pay()`, and a `[Shipped]` order behaves differently (no more `cancel()`) than a `[Created]` one.

The test to apply before drawing one: can you name at least two transitions that are illegal from some state but legal from another? If every transition is legal from every state, you don't have a state machine — you have a label that changes, and a state diagram would be drawing structure that doesn't exist.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: drawing a state diagram for an entity that's really just a status enum with no transition logic
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "This entity has multiple named statuses, so it needs a state diagram."

**Why it's wrong:** having several status *values* isn't the same as having a state *machine*. If a `User.status` field can flip freely between `active`, `inactive`, and `suspended` in any direction with no restrictions and no behavior difference beyond the label, a diagram showing five states and every possible arrow between them adds visual complexity without adding information — it's just an enum wearing a diagram's clothes.

**Correct model:** draw a state diagram only when some transitions are genuinely forbidden or trigger real behavior differences. Otherwise, a one-line list of valid values (or the compare-style table from this topic) says everything the diagram would have, faster and more honestly.
